content: They collaborate with operators to resolve technical issues, deliver training, assess alternative technological solutions, recommend operational enhancements, assist in leak detection, and respond to natural disasters and other emergencies. In Peru, significant measures have been implemented to enhance the monitoring and regulation of water service provision in rural areas. Community-based organizations dominate the management model, with over 24,000 such organizations accounting for 92% of service providers as of October 2023. These organizations oversee the daily operations and maintenance of rural water services and receive technical support from nearly 1,000 local government outreach units, known as Municipal Technical Areas. Sector reforms have accelerated since the 2016 Framework Law on the Management and Provision of Sanitation Services, which introduced a new framework for efficient and sustainable rural water service management, revised monitoring and regulatory mandates, and policies to improve water quality and sanitation. The National Superintendence of Sanitation Services, established in 1992, initially focused on urban utilities but began progressively monitoring rural community-based organizations in 2016, adapting its approach to rural conditions. For instance, rural areas have a lower threshold for service quality, such as 18 hours of water supply per day compared to 24 hours in urban areas. The agency uses monitoring results to identify underperforming supplies, provides guidance for improvement, and publishes annual benchmarking reports. Moving forward, there is potential to expand rural water supply coverage and fully operationalize regulatory functions. In Zambia, substantial reforms have been undertaken to improve rural and small-town water supply services. Since 2018, 11 commercial utilities have been mandated to ensure safe and reliable service provision. Recognizing the need for a robust enabling environment, Zambia’s National Water Supply and Sanitation Council developed the Rural Water Supply and Sanitation: Framework for Provision and Regulation in 2018. This framework outlines the roles of various stakeholders, provides an implementation plan, and specifies budget requirements. It supports the National Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Programme (2019–2030), which aims to ensure sustainable and equitable access to safe water and sanitation for Zambia’s rural population. In Uganda, the community-based management system for rural water supply infrastructure has faced challenges, including prolonged downtimes and inadequate operations and maintenance. To address these issues, the Ministry of Water and Environment introduced a professionalized model called Community-Based Management Plus. This model delegates key maintenance and repair functions to area service providers, typically private operators, through performance contracts involving local governments and water boards. These providers employ local hand pump mechanics, offer training, source spare parts, and ensure preventive maintenance schedules are followed. One such provider, Whave Solutions, operates across 17 districts and manages over 3,000 hand pumps, achieving functionality rates of 94–97% and completing 90% of repairs within one day. This represents a significant improvement compared to non-professionalized community-based systems. The expansion of utility-managed rural and small-town water supply services is a critical development in many lowand middle-income countries, including Africa and Asia. This expansion occurs through various pathways, such as extending existing utilities into rural areas, establishing new rural utilities, and attracting private capital for new schemes. Examples include Rwanda’s Byumba Local Public-Private Partnership Model, Senegal’s Hydraulic Works Operating Company, Uganda’s umbrella water authorities, and Vietnam’s Centre for Rural Water Supply and Environmental Sanitation. Utility-managed services generally outperform traditional community-managed systems in metrics such as supply hours, water quality, and operational cost coverage. In New Zealand, the Water Services Act 2021 expanded the scope of regulated water supplies to include very small community supplies serving up to 25 people. This regulatory expansion requires approximately 75,000 additional facilities to register by 2025 and meet national drinking-water standards by 2028. Recognizing resistance from service providers, Taumata Arowai, New Zealand’s independent drinking-water regulator, engaged extensively with small water suppliers to understand their challenges and secure their participation. Draft standards and regulations were shared for feedback, leading to substantial revisions that reduced the scope of required activities while maintaining public health protections. These efforts are expected to increase compliance and maximize public health benefits. In Canada, there is currently no regulatory framework for drinking-water services for First Nations communities on reserves. The 2013 Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act was repealed due to concerns about inadequate funding, lack of recognition of Aboriginal water rights, and insufficient engagement. The Government of Canada is now developing new legislation in consultation with First Nations to establish national standards for drinking-water quality and wastewater management. The Atlantic First Nations Water Authority, established in 2018 as Canada’s first Indigenous-owned water utility, has been a key advocate for regulations and standards. It manages the operation, maintenance, and capital upgrades of centralized water and wastewater assets for participating First Nations in Atlantic Canada.
